title: CSS codes for Quantum Metrology with Discrete-time Error Correction
authors: Ugnė Liaubaitė, Debora Ramacciotti, Robert Raußendorf
abstract: The goal of quantum metrology is to estimate an unknown parameter with better-than-classical precision and, ideally, to attain Heisenberg scaling. In realistic settings, however, noise can substantially reduce this advantage and, in many cases, restore standard-quantum-limit-like performance. Preserving the quantum enhancement therefore requires noise-robust strategies, which can be implemented using quantum error correction. In this work, we develop and analyze a quantum-metrology protocol based on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. The main result is that, for noise perpendicular to the sensing Hamiltonian, discrete-time error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window whose duration depends on the correction frequency. It is further shown that recovery applied only after the sensing evolution provides no metrological advantage over the corresponding uncorrected noisy protocol in the setup considered here. An analytical framework is developed for arbitrary CSS codes and applied to the Steane and Shor codes, for which the discrete-time corrected dynamics, the Heisenberg-like-to-SQL-like crossover, and the optimal interrogation time are determined and numerically analysed.
summary: This work analyzes quantum metrology protocols using CSS codes to estimate parameters with high precision despite environmental noise. By implementing discrete-time error correction, the authors show that the Heisenberg scaling advantage is maintained over a finite time window. The findings provide a detailed theoretical understanding of the trade-off between noise suppression and the ultimate achievable measurement precision.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to maintain the Heisenberg scaling advantage in quantum metrology when noise is present, requiring the implementation of quantum error correction.
main_result: Discrete-time error correction using CSS codes successfully preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window, although asymptotic scaling is limited by residual decay.
method: The authors develop an analytical framework to model the noisy evolution using the Lindblad master equation and analyze the effect of discrete-time error correction cycles on the projector probability.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum sensing protocol using Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes to estimate an unknown parameter via a local Z Hamiltonian. Noise is modeled as perpendicular X-type noise, and the dynamics are analyzed using the Lindblad equation.
key_observables: Classical Fisher Information ($F_C$), sensitivity ($\delta\omega^{-1}$), and the projector probability $P_X(\omega, t)$.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($\gamma$), correction frequency ($	au$), interrogation time ($t$), and the code parameters ($[[n, k, d]]$).
main_assumptions: Error correction operations are assumed instantaneous and ideal; the analysis is restricted to a finite interrogation-time window.
figures_summary: Figures compare sensitivity envelopes under varying noise and correction parameters, showing the crossover from Heisenberg-like to SQL-like scaling.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the metrological goal and the noisy dynamics. It then develops the framework for discrete-time error correction using CSS codes, deriving the evolution of the projector probability. Finally, it analyzes the resulting sensitivity envelope, determining the optimal interrogation time and crossover behavior.
why_interesting: The explicit analysis of error correction protocols in the context of quantum sensing provides concrete, mathematically rigorous guidelines for designing robust quantum measurements, which is highly relevant for experimental quantum optics and AMO platforms.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Envelope of the frequency sensitivity under uncorrected Z noise. Rows correspond to the Steane and Shor codes and columns to different values of the noise strength γ. Solid, dashed, and dotted lines denote the encoded projector protocol, n independent |+⟩probes, and the n-qubit GHZ probe, respectively. The notation ϵ used in the figure corresponds to the noise strength, ϵ = γ.

FIG. 2. Projector probability PX(ω, t) under discrete X-error correction for the Steane code (left) and the Shor code (right), for different correction intervals τ at ω = 3. The dense appearance reflects the rapid parameter-dependent oscillations.

FIG. 3. Frequency-sensitivity envelopes under discrete X-error correction for the Steane code (left) and the Shor code (right). Colored markers denote the exact local maxima of δω−1, while the corresponding continuous curves show the fitted two-factor envelope given by Eq. (C23). The uncorrected encoded protocol and the GHZ probe are included as analytical benchmarks and are not part of the fit.

FIG. 4. Crossover from the Heisenberg-like to the SQL-like regime under discrete X-error correction for the Steane code (left) and the Shor code (right), for different correction intervals τ. The interrogation time topt(T) is optimized for the fixed final budget T. Colored dots show the numerical results, while solid curves show the fitted two-factor envelope. Beyond topt, the protocol is repeated at fixed interrogation time, producing the staircase behavior. Stars mark the numerically determined topt(T).
FIG. 5. Rescaled discrete-QEC sensitivity. The sensing-time budget is normalized by the numerically determined topt, and the sensitivity is normalized by its value at topt.
